doc.title: Bob Havens interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Listening to swing records and Tommy Dorsey
summary: Unaware of the Swing Era as such, he collects Goodman, Miller and Whiteman records; his teacher pushes Dorsey but it did not catch his ear.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well you were, let’s see, in the late 30s then and early 40s, you were a young boy, were you aware of the Swing era that was becoming —

I really wasn’t aware that it was a particularly new thing, the Swing Era. All I knew is what I heard on the records. I didn’t know what came before it, years before — I just started tuning my ear into what was happening in those days. And fortunately I did grow up in what we now consider the big band era in popular music. And I listened to many, many records, besides the real old stuff back in the ‘20s, of Paul Whiteman, I listened to Benny Goodman and of course in the ‘40s the Glenn Miller Band was popular, and all of the old big bands that became a popular item, I listened to on records. And I had quite a large record collection after nine or ten years of collecting my own things, after my mother and father already got started on it years ago. So I grew to like the popular music and I also, I really got tuned in to a lot of variety of music by recordings. And I took an © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

interest in the classical music. The only part of music I never really got interested in was the Opera singing. I never, well to this day I really don’t enjoy it to listen to it. But I do like the music that goes along with it see, and the orchestra I’m quite interested in. But I have an interest in the classics as well as the jazz that I picked up along the way. And I think I probably had a natural tendency to tune in on the jazz aspect of the music. I became interested in what the individuals were doing on these recording, like the trumpet or the trombone. And of course I heard a lot of Tommy Dorsey’s recordings but of course Tommy was not considered a jazz player. But my trombone teacher really kind of pushed that style a lot and wanted me to listen to a lot of Dorsey records. But I don’t know, it was pretty, but I just didn’t quite — it didn’t really catch my ear that much.
